33739: While hosting her own banquet for women, she refused the drunken king's command to appear in her crown to show the guests her beauty.
33741: The king's advisers warned her example would lead wives everywhere to despise their husbands, so a decree removed her as queen, opening the way for Esther.
33742: Vashti was the queen of Ahasuerus at the opening of the book of Esther. When the king, merry with wine, ordered her to appear before his guests, she refused. She was deposed, and the search for a new queen brought Esther into the palace.
33743: The text gives no reason for her refusal and no judgment on it; it reports the advisers' fear that other wives would follow her lead (Esth 1:17-18).
33744: Some midrash portrays her negatively, as a granddaughter of Nebuchadnezzar who mistreated Jewish women, and suggests she was asked to appear wearing only her crown (tradition, Babylonian Talmud Megillah 12b).
33746: Many readers see her as a woman of dignity who refused to be displayed as property, and contrast her open refusal with Esther's quieter strategy.
33748: Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris; some identify her with Vashti, others think Vashti is a figure of the story only (debated).
33749: Composed and unbending, a queen who answers a public humiliation with a short, firm no.
33751: Akkadian Sin-uballit, "Sin (the moon god) has given life"
33757: He was deeply displeased that someone had come to seek the welfare of Israel, and with Tobiah and Geshem mocked the builders and accused them of rebellion.
33758: Ridicules the wall and plots attack
33759: Before the army of Samaria he scoffed at "these feeble Jews". When the wall rose, he and allies plotted to attack, and Nehemiah posted armed guards.
33760: Tries to lure and discredit Nehemiah
33761: He invited Nehemiah four times to a meeting in the plain of Ono, sent an open letter alleging he wanted to be king, and with Tobiah hired a prophet to frighten him into hiding in the temple.
33763: A grandson of the high priest Eliashib had married Sanballat's daughter; Nehemiah drove him away.
33764: Sanballat was the Persian-appointed governor of Samaria, the province north of Judah, and Nehemiah's chief opponent. He mocked the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, threatened attack, spread rumours that Nehemiah planned rebellion, and tried to lure him into a trap. A fortified Jerusalem threatened his influence in the region.
33765: He is called the Horonite (Neh 2:10), perhaps from Beth-horon near Jerusalem or Horonaim in Moab (debated). His family was tied by marriage to the high priest's family (Neh 13:28).
33766: Most see the conflict as political: Samaria's governor had influence in Judah before Nehemiah came and lost it as Judah became a stronger province (scholarly-consensus on the broad picture).
33768: His tactics of mockery, threats, distraction and slander are often used as a study in the kinds of opposition faced by anyone doing a good work.
33769: A papyrus from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, dated 407 BC, refers to "Delaiah and Shelemiah, the sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria" (scholarly-consensus). Papyri from Wadi Daliyeh near Jericho show that later governors of Samaria in the 300s BC also bore the name Sanballat.
33770: Sneering and theatrical in public, smooth and conspiratorial in private, always framing his opposition as loyalty to the king.
33774: Ammon (Persian district east of the Jordan)
33777: Standing beside Sanballat he jeered that if even a fox climbed on the wall it would break it down.
33778: Uses family ties to pressure Nehemiah
33779: Many nobles of Judah were bound to him by oath because of marriages, and they reported his good deeds to Nehemiah while he sent letters to frighten him.
33780: Thrown out of the temple storeroom
33781: While Nehemiah was away, the priest Eliashib gave Tobiah a large room in the temple courts. On returning, Nehemiah threw his furniture out and had the rooms purified.
33782: Tobiah, called "the Ammonite" and "the servant", was an official, probably in charge of the Ammonite region, who joined Sanballat in opposing Nehemiah. He had a Yahwistic name, meaning "the LORD is good", and close marriage ties with Jerusalem's leading families, which made him an insider-outsider. Nehemiah eventually evicted him from a room in the temple itself.
33783: His son Jehohanan married the daughter of Meshullam, one of the wall builders, and Tobiah himself married into the family of Shecaniah (Neh 6:18). He was related to the priest Eliashib (Neh 13:4).
33784: "Servant" (Hebrew ʿebed) may be an official title, "servant of the king", rather than an insult. Many link him to the later Tobiad family, powerful in the Ammonite region in the 200s BC according to the Zenon papyri and the remains at Iraq al-Amir in Jordan; the family link is plausible but debated.
33785: Witty and cutting, with the easy confidence of a well-connected man who knows whom to write to and whom to flatter.
33787: Probably Babylonian, perhaps "Sin (or Shamash) protect the father" (uncertain)
33789: First governor of the returned exiles
33791: Cyrus had his treasurer count out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, 5,400 items of gold and silver, and give them to Sheshbazzar, prince of Judah, to bring to Jerusalem.
33793: Years later the elders told the Persian governor that Cyrus had made Sheshbazzar governor and that he had laid the foundation of the house of God.
33794: Sheshbazzar was the "prince of Judah" whom Cyrus made governor and entrusted with the temple treasures for the first return from Babylon in 538 BC. He is said to have laid the temple's foundations. He then drops out of the story, and Zerubbabel leads the community. Who he was exactly is debated.
33795: Ezra 3 credits Zerubbabel and Joshua with laying the foundation (Ezra 3:8-10), while Ezra 5 credits Sheshbazzar (Ezra 5:16).
33797: Older commentators often held that Sheshbazzar was Zerubbabel's Babylonian name, which would explain why both are credited with the foundation. Critics note the Aramaic letter seems to speak of him as a figure of the past.
33799: Many scholars identify him with Shenazzar, son of King Jehoiachin (1 Chr 3:18), making him Zerubbabel's uncle. The names may be two spellings of one Babylonian name. This is debated.
33801: Others see him as a distinct Judean leader who began the work, with Zerubbabel later completing it under Darius.
33802: Dignified and careful, a steward who counts every bowl and knife twice before the long road home.
33803: Akkadian Tukultī-apil-Ešarra, "my trust is in the son of Esharra"
33807: Founder of the Assyrian empire's western expansion
33809: As "Pul" he came against Israel; Menahem paid him a thousand talents of silver, raised by a levy on wealthy men, to secure his own throne.
33811: Attacked by Aram and Israel, Ahaz of Judah sent temple silver and gold, calling himself the Assyrian king's "servant and son". Chronicles adds that the alliance brought Judah trouble rather than strength.
33813: In the days of Pekah he captured towns of northern Israel, Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali, and deported their people to Assyria, along with Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh.
33815: He took Damascus, deported its people and killed King Rezin. Ahaz went to meet him there and copied the design of an altar he saw.
33816: Tiglath-pileser III, also called Pul, made Assyria a true empire. From 745 to 727 BC he turned conquered lands into provinces and moved whole populations to break resistance. He took tribute from Israel's king Menahem, answered Judah's King Ahaz's plea for help, captured Damascus, and stripped Israel of Galilee and Gilead. His campaigns began the end of the northern kingdom.
33817: Kings uses both names, Pul (2 Kgs 15:19) and Tiglath-pileser (2 Kgs 15:29). Chronicles lists "Pul king of Assyria" and "Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria" side by side (1 Chr 5:26), which most read as one person described twice. Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy belongs to the crisis that led Ahaz to call on him (Isa 7:1-17).
33819: Isaiah presents Assyria as "the rod of my anger", a tool God uses to judge his people and then holds to account for its own arrogance (Isa 10:5-15).
33820: His royal annals and summary inscriptions from Nimrud (Calah) name Menahem of Samaria and Jehoahaz (that is, Ahaz) of Judah among tribute payers, and say that the Israelites overthrew Pekah and that he installed Hoshea as king (scholarly-consensus). A Babylonian king list records his rule in Babylon under the name Pulu, confirming that Pul and Tiglath-pileser are the same king (scholarly-consensus).
33821: Clipped and imperious, a conqueror who counts kingdoms in talents and deportees and speaks of kings as servants.
33827: Hoshea of Israel paid tribute, then stopped and sought help from Egypt. Shalmaneser imprisoned him, besieged Samaria for three years, and the city fell in Hoshea's ninth year.
33828: Shalmaneser V, son of Tiglath-pileser III, ruled Assyria from 727 to 722 BC. When King Hoshea of Israel rebelled, he imprisoned him and laid siege to Samaria for three years. Samaria fell in 722 BC, ending the northern kingdom, though historians debate whether he or his successor Sargon II completed the conquest.
33829: Kings says "the king of Assyria" took Samaria and deported Israel (2 Kgs 17:6); it names Shalmaneser as the besieger (2 Kgs 18:9) and leaves the conqueror's name ambiguous.
33831: One view: Shalmaneser took the city in 722 BC, as the Babylonian Chronicle's note that he "ravaged Samaria" suggests, and died soon after. Another: Sargon II, who claims the conquest in his inscriptions, captured or recaptured it about 720 BC after a revolt. Many historians combine the two. This is debated.
33832: Few inscriptions survive from his short reign. The Babylonian Chronicle records that he ravaged the city of Šamara'in, usually identified with Samaria (scholarly-consensus on the reading, some debate on the identification). Josephus (*Antiquities* 9.283-287) preserves a tradition of his campaign against Tyre.
33833: Stern and methodical, the voice of a siege commander prepared to wait three years.
33837: His general takes Ashdod; Isaiah walks barefoot
33838: When Sargon's commander (the tartan) captured Ashdod, Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign that Egypt and Cush, whom Judah hoped would help, would be led away captive by Assyria.
33839: Sargon II ruled Assyria from 722 to 705 BC and was the father of Sennacherib. He claims to have conquered Samaria and deported over 27,000 Israelites, and he crushed revolts in Philistia, including at Ashdod in 711 BC. The Bible names him only once, in Isaiah 20. For centuries he was known only from that verse, until his palace was found in the 1840s.
33840: Isaiah 20:1 is the only place Scripture names him, dating Isaiah's sign-act to the year Sargon's commander took Ashdod.
33841: Many believe the unnamed "king of Assyria" who resettled foreigners in Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24) was Sargon, since his inscriptions describe bringing in other peoples (scholarly-consensus that Sargon did so; whether 2 Kgs 17:24 refers only to him is debated).
33842: In 1843 the French consul Paul-Émile Botta excavated Sargon's capital, Dur-Sharrukin (modern Khorsabad), confirming a king known before only from Isaiah. His inscriptions claim the capture of Samaria and the deportation of 27,290 people (some copies 27,280), and describe the Ashdod campaign (scholarly-consensus on what the texts say; whether he or Shalmaneser V first took Samaria is debated).
33843: Boastful and precise, reciting numbers of captives and conquered cities like entries in a ledger.
33849: Records the reigns of Solomon, Rehoboam and Abijah
33850: Chronicles cites "the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam", the records of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer for Rehoboam, and "the midrash (story) of the prophet Iddo" for Abijah.
33851: Iddo was a seer at the court of Judah in the time of Solomon, Rehoboam and Abijah. Chronicles cites his writings as sources three times, but none of them has survived. He shows that prophets also served as recorders of royal history. He is not the same person as Iddo the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah (Zech 1:1; Ezra 5:1).
33852: He is known only as an author whose works the Chronicler consulted (2 Chr 9:29; 2 Chr 12:15; 2 Chr 13:22).
33853: Some rabbinic and later sources identify him with the unnamed "man of God from Judah" who rebuked Jeroboam at Bethel (1 Kgs 13:1-10), linking him to Jeroboam through Josephus's name Jadon (tradition, uncertain).
33854: Observant and deliberate, a court historian who speaks like a man writing everything down.
33858: Persuades Israel to free Judean captives
33859: When Pekah's army returned with 200,000 captives from Judah, Oded met them at Samaria and warned that God was angry at their excess and that they too were guilty. Leaders of Ephraim agreed; the captives were clothed, fed, anointed, and returned to Jericho.
33860: Oded was a prophet in Samaria during the war of Israel and Aram against King Ahaz of Judah, around 734 BC. When Israel's army brought home a huge number of Judean captives, Oded confronted them: they had gone beyond judgment into cruelty. Remarkably, they listened, and the captives were cared for and sent home. Many see the scene behind Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan.
33861: His speech calls the captives "your brethren" (2 Chr 28:11). The released captives were brought to Jericho, the city of palm trees (2 Chr 28:15). He is different from Oded the father of the prophet Azariah (2 Chr 15:1), although the Hebrew of 2 Chr 15:8 confusingly calls that prophecy "of Oded the prophet".
33862: Many commentators note the parallels with the Good Samaritan: Samaritans, wounded people clothed, anointed, carried on donkeys toward Jericho (Luke 10:30-35). Whether Jesus intended the echo is debated.
33863: Bold but appealing to conscience, a prophet who speaks to a victorious army as fellow sinners.
33868: Rebukes Asa for relying on Aram
33869: When Asa paid Ben-hadad of Aram to attack Israel, Hanani told him he had relied on the king of Aram rather than the LORD, and reminded him that "the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth" to support those whose hearts are true. From then on Asa would have wars.
33871: Asa was enraged and put Hanani in the stocks, and oppressed some of the people at the same time.
33872: Hanani was a seer who rebuked King Asa of Judah for trusting a foreign alliance instead of God. Asa had him locked in the stocks, making Hanani one of the first prophets imprisoned for his message. His son Jehu also became a prophet. He is not the Hanani who was Nehemiah's brother (Neh 1:2).
33873: He is called "the seer" (2 Chr 16:7) and is the father of the prophet Jehu (1 Kgs 16:1; 2 Chr 19:2).
33874: The date of Asa's 36th year (2 Chr 16:1) is a known chronological problem, since Baasha of Israel died earlier on the usual dating. Some count the years from the division of the kingdom, putting the events around 895 BC (debated).
33875: Unflinching and plain, speaking the hard truth to a king who had once been faithful.
33882: He told Baasha king of Israel that because he walked in the ways of Jeroboam, his house would be swept away like Jeroboam's. It happened under Baasha's son Elah.
33884: When Jehoshaphat returned from fighting alongside Ahab, Jehu asked him, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?" but also commended the good in him.
33886: The acts of Jehoshaphat were written in "the book of Jehu son of Hanani", included in the book of the kings of Israel.
33887: Jehu son of Hanani was a prophet whose ministry spanned decades and both kingdoms. He announced the downfall of Baasha's dynasty in Israel and later challenged King Jehoshaphat of Judah for allying with Ahab. He also wrote a history of Jehoshaphat's reign. He should not be confused with Jehu the king of Israel.
33888: He is the son of the seer Hanani (1 Kgs 16:1). His long career, from Baasha to Jehoshaphat, covers roughly forty years.
33889: Grave and balanced, rebuking firmly while acknowledging what is good.
33891: Prophecy by the Spirit of God
33893: The Spirit of God came on him and he met Asa returning from battle: "The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you." He urged the king to be strong because his work would be rewarded.
33895: Taking courage, Asa removed idols from Judah and Benjamin, repaired the altar, and gathered the people, including many from the north, to renew the covenant to seek the LORD.
33896: Azariah son of Oded was a prophet who met King Asa after a military victory and called him to keep seeking God. His message, "if you seek him, he will be found by you", led Asa to remove idols and lead the nation in renewing its covenant with God.
33897: He is the only person in Scripture to whom this exact prophecy is credited (2 Chr 15:1). The Hebrew of 2 Chr 15:8 reads "the prophecy of Oded the prophet", which many translations correct to "Azariah son of Oded" following ancient versions (debated textual point).
33898: Warm and urgent, the voice of someone pressing a good king to keep going while the moment lasts.
33902: Alternative date for the division of the kingdom
33905: Rehoboam gathered 180,000 men to fight the northern tribes, but Shemaiah brought God's word: "You shall not fight against your brothers... this thing is from me." They obeyed and went home.
33906: Calls Rehoboam to repent during Shishak's invasion
33907: When Pharaoh Shishak invaded, Shemaiah told Rehoboam and his princes they had abandoned God. They humbled themselves, and God granted partial deliverance, though Judah became subject to Egypt.
33909: Rehoboam's history was written in the records of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer.
33910: Shemaiah was a prophet in the reign of Rehoboam, Solomon's son. When the kingdom split, he stopped Rehoboam from going to war against the northern tribes, saying the division was God's doing. Later, when Egypt invaded, he called the king and leaders to humble themselves. He also kept a record of Rehoboam's reign. Several other men named Shemaiah appear in the Bible, including a false prophet in exile (Jer 29:24-32) and a hired prophet who tried to scare Nehemiah (Neh 6:10-13).
33911: He is called "the man of God" (1 Kgs 12:22). Egypt's invasion is dated to Rehoboam's fifth year (2 Chr 12:2).
33912: Shishak is usually identified with Pharaoh Sheshonq I, whose relief at Karnak in Egypt lists towns he conquered in the region (scholarly-consensus on the identification; the precise list and route are debated).
33913: Short and authoritative, delivering God's word in a sentence and expecting it to settle the matter.
33916: After his father Jehoiada died, King Joash and the officials turned to idols. The Spirit of God came on Zechariah and he warned them: "Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you." At the king's command they stoned him in the temple court. Dying, he said, "May the LORD see and avenge."
33918: Jesus speaks of the blood of all the righteous "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah", killed between the altar and the sanctuary.
33919: Zechariah was a priest, the son of the high priest Jehoiada who had saved and raised young King Joash. After Jehoiada died, Joash drifted into idolatry. When Zechariah warned him, the king had him stoned to death in the temple courtyard, forgetting all Jehoiada had done for him. Jesus probably refers to him as the last martyr in the Hebrew Bible's order of books.
33920: Joash "did not remember the kindness" of Jehoiada (2 Chr 24:22). Within a year Aramean forces struck Judah, and Joash was killed by his own servants "for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest" (2 Chr 24:23-25).
33922: Jesus refers to this Zechariah. Abel is the first murder in Genesis and Zechariah the last in Chronicles, which closes the Hebrew Bible, so "from Abel to Zechariah" means "from first to last". Matthew's "son of Barachiah" may be a blending with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zech 1:1), or a copyist's addition (Luke lacks it). The details are debated.
33924: Some identify Jesus' Zechariah with the post-exilic prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah, for whose martyrdom there is no biblical record; a few have suggested Zechariah son of Baris, killed in the temple in AD 68 according to Josephus (*Jewish War* 4.335-344), which would make Jesus' words a prophecy (speculative).
33925: Talmudic legend says his blood kept seething in the temple until the Babylonian conquest (tradition, Babylonian Talmud Gittin 57b).
33926: Fearless and grieved, a priest who speaks as one betrayed by a family friend, ending not with a curse of his own but a plea for God to see.
33933: With Bildad and Zophar he came to mourn with Job. They sat in silence with him seven days and nights, seeing how great his suffering was.
33934: First speech: the innocent do not perish
33935: He gently reminds Job that he has counselled others, asks who innocent ever perished, describes a night vision teaching that no mortal is pure before God, and urges Job to accept God's discipline.
33937: He accuses Job of undermining religion with his words, and finally lists sins Job must have committed, such as stripping the poor and refusing water to the thirsty, before urging him to return to God.
33939: God tells Eliphaz that his anger burns against him and his two friends because they have not spoken of God what is right, as Job has. They must offer sacrifices and Job will pray for them.
33940: Eliphaz from Teman in Edom is the first and apparently the eldest of Job's three friends. He begins kindly but holds firmly to the belief that suffering is God's response to sin, and as Job protests his innocence, Eliphaz grows harsher until he accuses Job of crimes without evidence. At the end God says he and his friends did not speak rightly about God.
33941: Teman was known for wisdom (Jer 49:7). An Eliphaz is also Esau's son, whose son was Teman (Gen 36:10-11), which may hint at the Edomite setting. His words are sometimes true in themselves; Paul quotes one line, "He catches the wise in their own craftiness" (Job 5:13; 1 Cor 3:19).
33943: Eliphaz represents traditional retribution theology: the righteous prosper and the wicked suffer. The book shows that this is not a full account of how God works.
33945: Some note that many of his statements echo Proverbs and the Psalms. His fault lies in applying general truths to Job's case without knowing the facts, which turns comfort into accusation.
33946: Polished, fatherly and sure of himself, speaking in proverbs and visions, gradually losing patience with a friend who will not accept his diagnosis.
33948: Shuah (perhaps a people descended from Abraham and Keturah)
33950: He insists God does not pervert justice, suggests Job's children died for their own sin, and urges Job to appeal to the wisdom of past generations.
33951: The fate of the wicked; no man is clean
